parsed.main_gap: Negative values of g are never excluded; §3 only rules out two distinct positive values, then silently assumes V ⊆ {0,c}. (Repairable in one line via f>0 and iterating (4).)

errors.description: The dichotomy after §3 is unjustified: showing V has at most one positive element does not give V ⊆ {0,c}, since g(x)=f(x)-x may a priori be negative (only g(x)>-x is noted). The arithmetic-progression argument of §3 also assumes c1,c2>0. A short argument (g(u)=c<0 forces u+nc=f^n(u)>0 for all n, absurd) is missing.
errors.quote:
Thus $V$ contains **at most one** positive number.  Consequently, either  

* (i) $g\equiv 0$ (constant), which gives $f(x)=x$, a solution; or  
* (ii) there is $c>0$ such that $V \subseteq \{0, c\}$ with both values attainable.

errors.description: Sign/typo in the expansion of A(x,y) for a=0,b=c: from the general formula the term is +4by = 4cy, not 4cx. Harmless since the inequality is only claimed to hold trivially, but it is an error in the displayed identity.

Case bookkeeping in §7 is loose: S_0=∅ was derived inside the contradiction hypothesis (ii) (both 0 and c attained), so the conclusion should be phrased as elimination of case (ii), leaving V={0} or V={c}. The final answer is nonetheless correct.
errors.quote: Since $S_0 = \emptyset$, the function $g$ never takes the value $0$.  Together with §3 this forces $g(x) \equiv c$

parsed.notes: Correct answer and a genuinely correct main line: (3)/(4), the identities (5)–(7), the density argument, Lemma 1 and the covering argument are all sound. Only the unhandled possibility of negative g prevents a 7.
